title: Governing Reserves: Managerial Discretion and Government Creditworthiness
authors: Sharon N. Kioko; Temirlan T. Moldogaziev
affiliations: Daniel J. Evans School of Public Policy and Governance University of Washington Seattle Washington USA; Paul H. O'Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs Indiana University Bloomington Indiana USA
abstract: ABSTRACT A government's ability to generate surpluses and build reserves reflects prudent financial management, with the accumulation of reserves signaling sound budgeting practices. Reserves are essential for sound fiscal governance during economic downturns, and managerial discretion over these resources is crucial to minimizing disruptions in service delivery. While the counter‐cyclical benefits of formal reserves are well documented, less attention has been paid to the discretion managers retain over reserves. Using credit ratings as a proxy for creditworthiness, we find that managerial discretion over accumulated resources enhances fiscal flexibility and strengthens creditworthiness; however, the presence of formal reserves alone does not improve credit ratings. Our study contributes to an emerging literature exploring whether better financial reporting can help us understand the critical balance between management flexibility and accountability mechanisms in public‐sector organizations.

title: Promises, Threats, and Norms: A Mixed Methods Study on Bureaucratic Support for Public Participation
authors: Jesse W. Campbell; Oscar Radyan Danar; Sanjay K. Pandey
affiliations: Department of Public Administration Incheon National University Incheon South Korea; Department of Public Administration, Faculty of Administrative Sciences Brawijaya University Malang Indonesia; Trachtenberg School of Public Policy and Public Administration George Washington University Washington DC USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Public participation can enhance policy quality and democratic legitimacy but may threaten bureaucratic control. We hypothesize that bureaucratic support for participation is higher when policies are less complex and participants are broadly representative. Using a mixed‐methods design involving Indonesian local public servants, we pursue complementarity by combining a 2 × 2 vignette‐based survey experiment with a Gioia analysis of qualitative reflections to explain the experimental results and further illuminate how bureaucrats evaluate participation. The experiment shows that participant representativeness significantly increases support, whereas policy complexity has no statistically significant effect. Integrating the experimental and qualitative data through joint displays reveals that bureaucrats rejecting participation frequently cite participant‐related risks, whereas supporters emphasize instrumental, procedural, and implementation benefits. Normative values, such as citizens' rights and democratic principles, are acknowledged regardless of bureaucrats' overall support. We conclude that bureaucratic support for public participation reflects how officials balance its promises, threats, and normative foundations.

title: Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems
authors: Benjamin Legros
affiliations: SKEMA Business School, Université Côte d’Azur, 92150 Paris, France
abstract: Why Larger Service Systems Benefit More from Scale How much extra demand can a service system handle when capacity is increased while keeping the same target level of customer blocking? In the paper “Convexity of Inverse Blocking Curves in Loss Systems,” Benjamin Legros establishes an exact economies-of-scale result for loss systems. The paper proves that the maximum supportable demand is an increasing and globally convex function of the number of servers. In practical terms, as a system becomes larger, each additional server can support progressively more additional demand while maintaining the same blocking target. Equivalently, the extra capacity required to accommodate additional demand decreases as the system grows. The result provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for resource pooling in capacity-constrained services. It applies to the classical Erlang-B loss model and extends to systems with a finite waiting room, with potential relevance for telecommunications, healthcare, emergency response, and other service operations.

title: The Effect of Small Quasi-Cash Rewards on Prosocial Behavior: The Case of Voluntary Plasma Donations
authors: Stijn Bruers; Erwin Ooghe; Erik Schokkaert
affiliations: Department of Economics, KU Leuven, 3000 Leuven, Belgium; Department of Economics, KU Leuven, 3000 Leuven, Belgium; and CESifo, 81679 Munich, Germany
abstract: To better understand how prosocial behavior can be effectively encouraged, we study four unresolved issues: whether small rewards also motivate prosocial behavior, how short-term effects differ from longer-run behavioral adjustments, whether incentives induce substitution away from other prosocial activities, and whether reminders about existing rewards meaningfully influence behavior. We examine these issues in a long-run randomized field experiment across 12 donation centers of the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders. Donors normally receive one thank-you-coupon (worth €1.5) for a blood donation and two coupons for a plasma donation. Informing donors about the existing rewards increases plasma donations by 4.6% during the nine-month information period, although this effect fades with repeated reminders. Rewarding plasma donors with an extra coupon raises plasma donations by an additional 7.1% during the six-month reward period; this effect grows during the reward period but disappears immediately afterward. We also document a substitution effect; the plasma reward reduces blood donations by 3.3%. Survey evidence suggests that small rewards act as signals of increased need or as gifts eliciting reciprocity and that our findings may extend to volunteering decisions more broadly. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, Behavioral Economics and Decision Analysis. Funding: This paper is based on research funded by the Belgian Red Cross-Flanders; the content reflects solely the views of the authors and not those of the Red Cross. title: Improper guilt: On exceptional postponements in the formal manufacture of criminals
authors: Nicolas Carrier; Jeffrey Monaghan
affiliations: Institute of Criminology & Criminal Justice, Carleton University, Ottawa, Canada
abstract: The sociology of law has not yet taken stock of the crucial role played by the admission of guilt in summary justice: it allows criminal law to absolve itself from the violence it employs to manufacture criminals and produce “just” punishments. Relying on some elements of Luhmann’s sociological theory, our thesis proposes that, in summary justice, the admission of guilt deparadoxifies legal self-referentiality, allowing criminal law to maintain a blind spot on the violence that precedes punishment. This thesis was developed following the observation of peculiar courtroom decisions, undocumented in the academic literature: exceptional instances where individuals are maintained in a state of pre-penal legal ensnarement on the grounds of an improper admission of guilt.

title: Victims’ relational work in online investment fraud
authors: Ran Ren; Yun Ai
affiliations: Department of Sociology, Chengdu University of Technology, China; School of Sociology and Psychology, Central University of Finance and Economics, Beijing, China
abstract: Victims’ participation in online investment frauds is not just justified by egoist desire or greed, but also changing relational frames under uncertainty and ambiguity. Drawing on the concept of relational work from economic sociology, this paper examines how victims of the ‘China–Africa Mining Corporation’ fraud justify and sustain their participation in such a crime of interaction. Based on two years of digital fieldwork, we trace victims’ in situ experiences across three stages of participation. First, victims overcame the uncertainty of investing by drawing on personal relationships and state-sanctioned narratives to construct trust. Second, those who became referrers framed recruitment as an act of care, staking their own credibility on the scheme’s legitimacy. Third, as returns failed to materialise, victims sustained belief through practices of patience, loyalty, and moral affirmation. The paper extends the application of relational work theory to cybercrime and demonstrates how victims’ relational work rendered participation meaningful and defensible.

title: The conversion of capital across fields: Hysteresis and the integration paradox among British Muslims
authors: Tahir Abbas
affiliations: Aston University, Birmingham, UK; Centre on Radicalisation, Inclusion and Social Equity, Birmgham, UK
abstract: The integration paradox – heightened exclusion among the most socio-economically integrated members of some, though not all, minority communities – challenges linear models of incorporation. This article reconceptualises the paradox through a Bourdieusian field-analytic lens, using latent profile analysis of UK survey data (N = 2535, including 109 Muslim respondents) to identify four configurations of belonging: Adaptive Mainstreamers, Empowered Pluralism, Individualised Assimilation and Double Alienation. British Muslims attain the capital-rich Empowered Pluralism configuration at least as often as others, yet report humiliation at nearly three times the odds of non-Muslims in the same configurations – a misrecognition gap concentrated among Adaptive Mainstreamers and absent within Empowered Pluralism, suggesting strongly resourced dual belonging operates protectively. Employment predicts capital-rich belonging only among respondents below their mid-fifties, consistent with hysteresis in capital convertibility. Heterogeneity analyses confine Double Alienation to foreign-born Muslims. The findings relocate the paradox from average attitudes to misrecognition at equal capital.

title: Enterprise Architecture Threat Modeling for Cybersecurity Risk Management
authors: Branko S. Bokan; Joost Santos
affiliations: The George Washington University Washington District of Columbia USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Organizations invest heavily in cybersecurity capabilities, yet the relationship between deployed defensive portfolios, practitioner judgments of coverage, and empirically observed adversary behavior remains difficult to assess. This study examines that relationship by integrating practitioner elicitation with threat‐informed cybersecurity architecture analysis. A model‐derived analytical baseline was constructed using the Cybersecurity Architecture Review (CAR) methodology aligned with MITRE ATT&CK version 17, quantifying protect, detect, and respond coverage for 12 commonly deployed cybersecurity capability categories. Survey data from 65 cybersecurity practitioners were used to characterize capability portfolios, perceived coverage, and factors influencing capability‐selection decisions. Results show uneven modeled coverage across the ATT&CK lifecycle and substantial functional overlap among capability categories. Across 910 respondent‐tactic observations, practitioner‐estimated coverage exceeded corresponding respondent‐specific modeled coverage by approximately 27 percentage points on average, although the magnitude and direction of perception‐model divergence varied by tactic. Most subgroup comparisons by professional role, responsibility, and experience did not identify statistically significant differences, while government respondents exhibited slightly higher mean divergence than nongovernment respondents in one pairwise comparison. Capability‐selection decisions reflected multiple organizational and external influences, with formal internal threat modeling reported less frequently than peer practices, regulatory or compliance requirements, independent research, and analyst or consultant reports. The findings demonstrate how threat‐informed architecture analysis can complement practitioner judgment by making modeled coverage, gaps, overlap, and divergence explicit within organizational cybersecurity risk governance.

The Participation Gap: Reproducing Socioeconomic Inequality in Workplace Participation
authors: Jan Simon Danko
affiliations: University of Zurich, Switzerland
abstract: While workplace participation is widely endorsed as both a democratic ideal and a managerial imperative, access to it remains unequally distributed. Drawing on a Bourdieu-inspired organisational field perspective, this study examines how perceived inequalities in workplace participation are structured by class-based capital distributions and classed dispositions that align, or fail to align, with dominant organisational norms. Using original survey data from Switzerland, the article finds that individuals with higher socioeconomic standing report significantly greater access to workplace participation, even after accounting for their hierarchical position, educational attainment, and conventional sociodemographic factors. This relationship is mediated by classed dispositions differentially attuned to the rules of the game in the organisational field. The article thus challenges the normative assumption that participation inherently promotes equality, demonstrating that it can reproduce rather than redress social inequalities when underlying structural imbalances remain unaddressed.

title: Algorithmic management and the spatiotemporality of workarounds
authors: Lakshmi Narasimha Raju Vuddaraju; Sarah Hudson; Yi Liu
affiliations: Rennes School of Business, France
abstract: Existing literature on algorithmic management has explored how workers respond to algorithmic control using workarounds. However, the role of spatiotemporal factors in shaping these workarounds is largely overlooked. This study therefore examines how workers use spatiotemporal workarounds in response to algorithmic management. We integrate Lefebvre’s spatial triad and rhythmanalysis to analyse data from an online community of Amazon delivery drivers. Our findings show how delivery drivers proactively adapt to spatiotemporal constraints imposed by algorithms by modifying their routes, adjusting the pace and rhythm of their work and using workarounds to proactively influence future algorithmic decisions. Our study contributes to the growing literature on the spatiotemporality of algorithmic work, highlights the role of humans as proactive agents in shaping algorithmic decisions and exerting temporal sovereignty and reconceptualises workarounds as dynamic, evolving and future-oriented adaptations rather than immediate resistance tactics.

title: Ownership and Confusion in Employee‐Owned Firms: An Exploration of the EOT Model
authors: Jonathan Preminger; Dimitrinka Stoyanova Russell
affiliations: Cardiff Business School Cardiff University Cardiff UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Based on interviews with employees in UK employee ownership trusts (EOTs), this article interrogates understandings of ‘ownership’ and explores confusion, tensions and frustrations in the lived experience of ownership stemming from employees' dual status as employees and owners. Employees assume that ownership brings various rights, but these often conflict with management understandings, the perspectives of other employees and the limited rights legally embedded in the EOT model. This emphasises the tensions between employee‐owners' legal status as beneficiaries and aspects of their ownership status that are dependent on norms and discourse. Relationships are crucial in developing shared understandings of ownership within the internal ‘community’ of employee‐owners. By showing how relationships shape such understandings and how ownership ‘works’ in practice, the study illuminates how conceptualisations of ownership impact the functioning of EOT firms.

title: Ownership, Diversity and the Effectiveness of Government‐backed Financial Support during a Systemic Crisis: Evidence from One Million UK SMEs
authors: Ahmed Barakat; Meryem Duygun; Maurizio Fiaschetti; Eddie Gerba; Tian Han; Enrico Onali; Afshin Sabri; Mike Tsionas; Huamao Wang
affiliations: University of Nottingham; UCL Institute of Finance and Technology; Bank of England, London School of Economics and CES Ifo; University of Bristol; Lloyds Banking Group plc; Lancaster University
abstract: Abstract Using proprietary data on over one million UK Small and Medium‐Sized Enterprises (SMEs) from 2017 to 2024, we examine how ownership composition and director diversity condition the impact of government‐backed Covid‐19 loan programmes on normal (non‐Covid) loan default outcomes. Building on the Behavioural Theory of the Firm and the Attention‐Based View, we develop Attention‐Based Governance (ABG) as a conceptual lens for explaining how SMEs deploy government‐backed slack during systemic crises. Our results show that SMEs with multiple owners from the same family are more effective than single‐owner SMEs in managing Covid support, indicating stronger internal collective oversight and discipline. Furthermore, SMEs with domestic institutional owners and female directors exhibit stronger capability and discipline, while those with foreign institutional owners or foreign directors display higher default risk on normal loans. Additional analysis reveals that foreign‐owned firms are least likely to default on the government‐backed Covid loans themselves. This finding reflects the selective allocation of managerial attention towards highly visible, publicly guaranteed debt to protect reputational capital with global stakeholders. Overall, our study shows how ownership composition and director diversity direct managerial attention and determine whether public funding leads to stronger financial resilience or heightened default risk at the firm level.

Service Recovery in Chatbot‐mediated Environments: Trust Dynamics and Customer Loyalty Intentions
authors: Wilson Ozuem; Silvia Ranfagni; Michelle Willis
affiliations: University of Cumbria, Institute of Business, Industry and Leadership UK; University of Florence, Department of Economics and Business Sciences Italy; University of Roehampton, Faculty of Business and Law UK
abstract: Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

title:
New wine, old bottles? Effective strategies of new
                    <scp>GenAI</scp>
                    firms
authors: Kathleen M. Eisenhardt; Xilan Zhang
affiliations: Department of Management Science and Engineering Stanford University Stanford California USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Blending insights from GenAI, strategic reasoning, and empirical grounding in five illustrative ventures, we contribute a theoretical framework for effective strategies of new GenAI firms. They face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory) such that two complementary strategic logics —Process Perspective (PP) and Resource‐based View (RBV)—are relevant. Second, we identify process‐based (i.e., well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. Some relate to GenAI, some generalize. Third, we address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI, technology strategy when there is upstream technical dominance and many downstream firms, and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software and predictive AI. Managerial Summary The rapid trajectory of GenAI is stunning. Yet many new GenAI firms are simply thin wrappers around well‐known LLMs. Drawing on five illustrative ventures, we contribute a framework for effective strategies for new GenAI firms. These firms face bifurcated uncertainty (i.e., high uncertainty of a nascent market, moderate uncertainty of a somewhat predictable technology trajectory). This calls for creating advantage by navigating high uncertainty markets to accomplish key strategic tasks and relying on foresight to build strategically valuable resources. Specifically, we identify process‐based (well‐designed business model and product innovation process) and resource‐based (i.e., superior data, efficient orchestration, complementary resources) advantages. We also address what is unique about GenAI entrepreneurship, including strategic implications of GenAI and a cross‐technology comparison with technologies like software, predictive AI, and quantum.

title:
Whither business model innovation strategy in the age of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ?
authors: Christoph Zott; Raphael Amit
affiliations: IESE Business School Barcelona Spain; The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We argue that business models are transformed into auto‐adaptive systems through embedded AI inference and learning activities. The competitive advantage of focal firms may increasingly depend on how effectively their activity systems learn relative to competing business models, with learning serving as a meta value driver. Such learning‐based advantages may be difficult to replicate when they are costly to create, path dependent, anchored in distinctive accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. Entrepreneurs and corporate leaders thus become architects and curators of evolving learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance. Managerial Summary The competitive advantage of focal firms increasingly depends on new AI learning and inference activities, which serve as meta‐value drivers in business models that learn faster, more broadly, and more reliably than competing business models. These dynamic learning‐based advantages are difficult to replicate because they are costly, path dependent, anchored in specific accumulated data, and rely on tightly coupled recursive feedback loops among business model activities. In this paper we argue that entrepreneurs and corporate leaders need to become architects and curators of evolving, auto‐adaptive learning systems and innovators of novel business models that are critical to their firm's value creation and sustainable performance.

title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
authors: Rahul Kapoor; Manav Raj
affiliations: The Wharton School University of Pennsylvania Philadelphia Pennsylvania USA
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

title: TESTING FOR ENDOGENEITY: A MOMENT-BASED BAYESIAN APPROACH
authors: Siddhartha Chib; Minchul Shin; Anna Simoni
affiliations: WUSTL; Philadelphia Fed; CNRS
abstract: A standard assumption in the Bayesian estimation of linear regression models is that the regressors are exogenous in the sense that they are uncorrelated with the model error term. In practice, however, this assumption can be invalid. In this article, using the exponentially tilted empirical likelihood (ETEL) framework, we develop a Bayes factor test for endogeneity that compares a base model that is correctly specified under exogeneity but misspecified under endogeneity against an extended model that is correctly specified in either case. We provide a comprehensive study of the log-marginal ETEL. We demonstrate that our testing procedure is consistent from a frequentist point of view: as the sample grows, it almost surely selects the base model if and only if the regressors are exogenous, and the extended model if and only if the regressors are endogenous. The methods are illustrated with simulated data and problems concerning the causal effect of automobile prices on automobile demand and the causal effect of potentially endogenous airplane ticket prices on passenger volume.

title: China's sovereign debt market (1921–37): Information efficiency and the impact of rumours
authors: Dan Li; Yajie Wang; Yiran Xie; Zhihao Xu
affiliations: School of Economics Fudan University Shanghai China; International Business School Zhejiang Guangsha Vocational and Technical University of Construction Jinhua Zhejiang China; School of Economics University of Sydney Sydney Australia; Institute of Economics, School of Social Sciences Tsinghua University Beijing China
abstract: Abstract China's sovereign debt market emerged with the establishment of the Shanghai Chinese Merchant Stock Exchange (SCMSE) in 1921 during the Beijing Era (1912–27) and flourished in the Prewar Nanjing Era (1927–37), when it dominated the securities market. Despite this growth, our analysis of weekly SCMSE–traded debt returns shows that the market lacked even weak form efficiency throughout the period. This inefficiency fostered a rumour‐driven environment. Using Shenbao , we find that weekly rumours related to the debt market rose from 0.6 in the Beijing Era to 1.5 in the Nanjing Era, yet the Beijing market was more vulnerable to their influence. Positive rumours were ignored in both periods, whilst each negative rumour reduced weekly returns by 96 basis points in the Beijing Era, compared with only 53 basis points in the Nanjing Era. Both markets responded similarly to rumours later verified, yet the Nanjing market was far less unsettled by false reports. Taken together, the evidence suggests that by the Nanjing Era the sovereign debt market had developed greater resilience in processing information, marking a step towards improved efficiency.

title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
authors: TOBIAS J. MOSKOWITZ; CHASE P. ROSS; SHARON Y. ROSS; KAUSHIK VASUDEVAN
abstract: ABSTRACT Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.

title: The effect of the mandatory disclosure of corporate tax returns on reporting bias
authors: ERIC J. ALLEN; HENRY L. FRIEDMAN; AYDIN UYSAL
affiliations: UC Riverside; UCLA Anderson School of Management; Former Director of Equity Research at the Charles Schwab Corp. Deceased.
abstract: ABSTRACT How do investor reactions to the mandatory disclosure of firm tax information influence managers' reporting choices? To answer this question, we build a structural model of reporting bias, which we test with a unique data set of Turkish firms that have been mandated to publicly disclose their tax returns since 2009. We find that both book and tax income numbers are informative to investors. Structural estimates are consistent with disclosure of the tax report reducing both market incentives to manage book earnings and investor uncertainty about underlying firm value. Tax disclosure is associated with higher reported tax income, though the increase is not statistically significant. Counterfactual estimates suggest that book‐tax‐conformity could change financial and tax reporting biases, but lead to a lower quality information environment relative to the separate disclosure of book and tax reports.

title: Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
authors: John Gallemore; Vincent Giese
affiliations: University of North Carolina; University of Mannheim
abstract: ABSTRACT We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

title:
Would a Balanced
                    <scp>PCAOB</scp>
                    Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
authors: Yoon Ju Kang; M. David Piercey
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Amherst Amherst Massachusetts USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

title: Public Service Decline and Support for the Populist Right: Evidence from England’s National Health Service
authors: ZACHARY P. DICKSON; SARA B. HOBOLT; CATHERINE DE VRIES; SIMONE CREMASCHI
affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science; IE University; University of Oxford
abstract: The rise of populist right parties is well studied, but relatively little attention has been given to how public service performance influences voter support. Given that public services are often the primary means through which citizens interact with the state, we argue that declining public services can create grievances that increase the appeal of populist right parties. Focusing on England’s National Health Service, we combine administrative data on local health facility closures with panel data on public preferences and voting intentions. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that closures reduce satisfaction with public services and increase support for populist right parties. These effects are moderated by migrant registrations at local health practices, highlighting the interaction between public service performance and immigration concerns in fueling populist right support. Our findings underscore the role of public service decline as a driver of support for populist parties, especially in areas undergoing demographic change.
